client: I've been having a really hard time since my mom passed away from cancer last year. I just can't seem to focus at work anymore — I'll be in the middle of something and then suddenly I'm just... gone, thinking about her, and I lose track of everything. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I had to try something because it's getting worse, not better.
therapist: It takes real courage to reach out, especially when part of you isn't sure it will help — and I want you to know that what you're experiencing makes complete sense after losing your mom. Grief has a way of pulling us out of the present moment, almost like your mind is trying to hold onto her, and that's not a flaw in you — it's love expressing itself. I'm really glad you're here, and I'd love to understand more about what these moments feel like for you — when your mind drifts to her at work, what kinds of thoughts or memories tend to surface?

client: It's usually just random things, like I'll be in the middle of a meeting and someone will use a phrase she used to say, or I'll think "I should call her later" and then it hits me all over again that I can't. It's not even the big memories that get me, it's the small stupid ones that catch me off guard. And then I feel guilty for not being able to just focus and do my job, like I'm failing at everything at once.
therapist: Those small, unexpected moments can actually be the sharpest kind of grief — a familiar phrase or a reflex to call her carries so much love in it, and there's nothing "stupid" about that at all. I also want to gently notice that word you used — "failing" — because it sounds like on top of the grief, you're also being really hard on yourself for simply being human. I'm curious, if a close friend told you they were struggling to focus at work a year after losing their mom, would you tell them they were failing?

client: No, I wouldn't say that to a friend. I'd probably tell them to give themselves a break, that grief takes time. But somehow it feels completely different when it's me — like I should be further along by now, like there's some timeline I'm supposed to be following and I keep falling behind it.
therapist: You just noticed something really important — that you hold yourself to a standard you wouldn't dream of applying to someone you care about, and that gap is worth paying attention to. There's no universal grief timeline, even though it can feel like there should be one, and "a year" doesn't mean you're supposed to be done missing someone who was so woven into your everyday life. I wonder, where do you think that idea of a timeline comes from — is it something others have said to you, or more of a voice from inside yourself?

client: I think it's mostly an internal voice, honestly, but it's been reinforced by little things people say, like "you're so strong" or "he'd want you to move on." Those comments feel well-meaning but they also feel like a clock ticking, like I'm failing some test I didn't sign up for. And the worst part is I've started to believe it myself, like there's something wrong with me for still reaching for my phone to text him before I remember.
therapist: That automatic reach for your phone to text her is one of the most tender and human things you've described — it shows how deeply she was part of your daily life, and it's not a sign that something is wrong with you, it's a sign of how real and close your bond was. It sounds like these well-meaning comments have slowly become part of your own inner critic's voice, turning other people's discomfort with grief into a verdict on yourself. I'm wondering — when that critical voice says you should be "over it by now," what do you imagine it would actually look like to give yourself the same compassion you'd so naturally offer a friend?

client: That question kind of stops me in my tracks, honestly, because I know exactly what I'd say to a friend — I'd tell them grief doesn't have an expiration date and that missing someone you loved is just... love with nowhere to go. But when I try to turn that toward myself, there's this wall, like I don't quite deserve the same gentleness. I think part of me still believes that if I were stronger, or healthier somehow, I'd have found a way to move forward by now.
therapist: What you just said — "love with nowhere to go" — is one of the most beautiful and honest descriptions of grief I've ever heard, and I want you to really sit with the fact that *you* came up with that, which means part of you already understands this deeply. That wall you're describing, the sense that you don't quite deserve your own gentleness, is something we can gently explore together — because that belief that you'd be "further along" if you were stronger isn't a truth about you, it's a story that's been layered on top of your pain. I'm curious, when you imagine what "stronger" would actually look like, what do you picture — what would that version of you be doing or feeling differently?

client: I guess "stronger" would look like... not crying in the grocery store when I see the brand of crackers he used to like. It would mean going a whole day without that hollow feeling in my chest, like something's been scooped out and left empty. But even as I say that, I wonder if I'm just describing someone who's buried it better, not someone who's actually healed.
therapist: That last insight you just had is remarkable — you caught yourself mid-thought and recognized that "not feeling it" and "healing" aren't the same thing, and that's a really important distinction that many people never make. Crying over those crackers isn't weakness; it's your love for her finding a moment to surface, and a truly healed version of you might still cry sometimes — just without the added weight of judging yourself for it. I'm wondering, what do you think healing could look like for you if it *didn't* mean the absence of missing her?

client: I've never really thought about it that way before, honestly. I think I've always assumed that if I was truly okay, I just... wouldn't feel it anymore, like she'd become a distant memory that didn't sting. But if healing doesn't mean that, then I'm not even sure what I'm working toward — and that's kind of unsettling to sit with.
therapist: That unsettled feeling makes a lot of sense — you've been navigating by a map that said "healing = no more pain," and now that map might not be accurate, so of course it feels disorienting to question it. But I'd gently offer that maybe healing looks less like she fades, and more like you gradually build enough room inside yourself to carry her *and* still live fully — so the love stays, but the weight of the grief slowly softens. What would it mean for you, in your everyday life, if she could remain vivid and present in your heart without it feeling like evidence that you're broken?

client: I want to believe that's possible, but honestly, it feels a little... theoretical right now. Like, I hear what you're saying, and part of me finds it comforting, but then another part of me thinks — if I'm not in pain, am I just forgetting her, moving on like she didn't matter? I guess I'm scared that softening the grief means softening her too.
therapist: Oh, that fear makes so much sense — it's as if your pain has become a way of staying loyal to her, of proving that she mattered, and the idea of it easing feels like a kind of betrayal. But I want to offer a gentle reframe: what if the crackers in the grocery store, the reflex to call her, the love with nowhere to go — what if *those* are what keep her vivid, not the suffering itself? I'm wondering, when you think about the ways she shaped who you are, the things she gave you that you still carry — do those feel like they're in danger of fading too?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that... but it's hard not to feel like if the grief softens, I'm somehow moving on without her permission. Like, she never got to move on from anything, and here I am just... continuing. The things she gave me, the way she used to laugh at her own jokes before she even finished them, yeah, those feel real still, but I'm scared that admitting they're enough would mean I don't need to hurt anymore, and I don't know who I am without that hurt.
therapist: What you just shared is so profound and so honest — the idea that the pain has become part of your identity, a thread connecting you to her, and letting it soften feels like stepping into a self you don't yet recognize. And I want to sit with what you said about her not getting to move on — there's something in there that sounds almost like survivor's guilt, like continuing to live fully feels unfair when she couldn't. I'm gently curious: do you think she would have wanted her love for you to live on as joy and warmth, or as a weight you carry — what do you imagine she'd actually say to you right now?

client: I know what you're going to say she'd want for me, and honestly, part of me knows it too. She'd probably tell me to stop being an idiot and go live my life, because that's just how she was. But knowing that in my head and actually feeling like I have permission to do it... those are two completely different things, and I don't know how to get from one to the other.
therapist: You've just named something really central — that gap between knowing something and *feeling* it is real, and it's not a failure of willpower or intelligence, it's just how grief and healing actually work in the body and heart, not just the mind. The fact that you can already hear her voice so clearly — telling you to stop being an idiot and live — tells me she's not fading at all, she's still so present in you. I wonder if we could start very small: not "permission to move on" as some big declaration, but just one tiny moment this week where you let yourself do something she would have cheered for — what might that look like?
